He means: can he really be seeing Helena, whom he believed dead, or is an illusionist tricking his sight? The question registers the almost supernatural quality of Helena's return.

anchor_text: 'Tis but the shadow of a wife you see, the name, and not the thing
summary: Helena's first words on her reappearance are a riddle of her own: she is only a 'shadow' and a 'name,' not the 'thing' itself — meaning she has been a wife in name only (never consummated the marriage with Bertram's knowledge or consent) and is still only a shadow of a wife until Bertram fully and freely accepts her. The distinction between the name and the thing echoes legal and theological debates about what constitutes a true marriage.
detail: Helena deliberately echoes Diana's riddling mode, maintaining the enigma one beat longer before Bertram's 'Both, both; O, pardon!' resolves it. 'Shadow' carries Platonic overtones (appearance without substance) but also the theatrical sense of an actor or understudy who fills a role — fitting for a play saturated with substitution and doubles. The legal implication is precise: a marriage not consummated was dissoluble ('the name and not the thing').

anchor_text: Both, both; O, pardon!
summary: Bertram's two-word recognition — 'Both, both' — answers Helena's claim to be only shadow and name by insisting she is both the reality and the shadow, name and thing together. His 'O, pardon!' is the play's nearest approach to a direct apology. Critics have long debated whether this brief exclamation is adequate acknowledgement of his treatment of Helena, or whether its abruptness represents the play's refusal to provide the emotional resolution romance would normally demand.
detail: The abruptness of Bertram's acceptance is one of the central critical problems of All's Well. Unlike the source story in Boccaccio, where Beltramo's recognition and reformed love are at least briefly dramatised, Shakespeare gives Bertram three words. Whether this is deliberate alienation-effect, a failure of dramatic imagination, or a mark of the play's 'problem' quality is contested across modern criticism.

anchor_text: when I was like this maid I found you wondrous kind
summary: Helena reveals the bed-trick to Bertram: 'when I was like this maid' — disguised as, or substituting for, Diana — he was 'wondrous kind,' i.e., sexually tender or generous. She immediately produces the material proof: Bertram's ancestral ring and the letter containing his conditions ('When from my finger you can get this ring / And are by me with child').

Both conditions are now met: she has his ring and carries his child.

A 'Tom' was a common name for a nobody or a fool. The nickname encapsulates Parolles's character: he was exposed as all sound, no courage. anchor_text: If thou beest yet a fresh uncropped flower, choose thou thy husband
summary: The King's metaphor of Diana as a 'fresh uncropped flower' alludes to virginity through the standard Renaissance trope of the unplucked flower. 'Uncropped' means not yet gathered or harvested — still intact. The King is asking whether Diana is still a virgin; if so, she may choose her own husband and he will provide her dowry. The flower = virginity image was a commonplace from Ovid and the Latin lyric tradition through to contemporary English verse.
detail: The King's gesture is genuinely generous — offering Diana the choice of husband and a dowry — but it also illustrates how the play's resolution remains within a patriarchal framework where female chastity is the commodity that commands a reward. Diana's chastity is real (the bed-trick preserved it), but the King's phrasing reduces her heroic loyalty to a marketable attribute. The irony is characteristic of All's Well's 'problem play' quality: the happy ending is achieved but its terms are uncomfortable.

anchor_text: All yet seems well; and if it end so meet, the bitter past, more welcome is the sweet

anchor_text: The king's a beggar, now the play is done
summary: The King steps outside the fiction to deliver an Epilogue, speaking as an actor appealing directly to the audience for applause. 'The king's a beggar' inverts the play's social world: the most powerful character becomes a supplicant ('beggar') to the spectators, whose 'patient' silence and 'gentle hands' (applause) are the only payment the players seek. This is a conventional Elizabethan Epilogue device, asking the audience to 'express content' — show their approval.
detail: The Epilogue's move from story to metatheater was common in Shakespeare's comedies: the character who wielded most power within the fiction becomes the most dependent on the audience outside it. 'With strife to please you, day exceeding day' promises that the company will keep working to exceed themselves. The Epilogue may allude to a specific court or theatre performance and its expected fee of applause. Compare Prospero's Epilogue in The Tempest.
